 The Advancing Global Health Annual Program Statement (AGH/APS) Mechanism: Supplementing the America First MOUs 
 Authors: 
 Kellie Moss , Stephanie Oum , and Jennifer Kates 
 Published: 
 Nov 13, 2026 
 Print 
 Email 
 Copy Link 
 Add KFF on Google 
 Key Points
 In September 2025, the State Department released the America First Global Health Strategy (AFGHS), its new approach for U.S. engagement in global health, anchored to bilateral agreements negotiated directly with countries (through memoranda of understanding, or MOUs), although limited information is available on their status. To supplement and support MOU implementation, the State Department is also using an Annual Program Statement (APS) mechanism, an open-ended competitive funding opportunity, to solicit applications in support of AFGHS goals. To shed greater light on U.S. global health efforts under the AFGHS, this analysis examines the Advancing Global Health APS (AGH/APS) award opportunities announced to date by looking at how funding may be directed across countries and selected areas of global health programming, painting a fuller picture of how continued U.S. global health investment may look in a post-USAID foreign aid landscape.
 The State Department anticipates using the AGH/APS to provide up to $4.5 billion across four funding windows from March 2026 to February 2027. A range of entities are eligible to apply for funding, including governments and non-governmental organizations, and funding opportunities are made available through specific addenda.
 To date, 12 addenda have been released across three funding rounds, totaling up to $1.43 billion and representing up to 122 possible awards.
 Seven of the 12 are focused on specific MOU countries – Cameroon, Cote d’Ivoire, Malawi, Mozambique, Nigeria, the Philippines, and Uganda.
 Five are focused on specific health areas – child development, care, and protection; neglected tropical diseases (NTDs); nutrition; population-based surveys and surveillance; and rapid outbreak response (the NTDs and nutrition addenda identify specific geographic areas and countries for support).
 Objectives and activities across the addenda are varied and range from enhancing the delivery of health services across disease programs; supporting high-impact NTD interventions; strengthening the systems and workforce that protect vulnerable children through improved laws, policies, and services; and strengthening global health security through improved infection prevention and control, immunization for outbreak response, point-of-entry screening, and risk communication. Some addenda include mentions of key, focus, and vulnerable populations (including women and children, and people living with HIV, tuberculosis, and malaria).
 These findings provide insight into how the U.S. intends to further operationalize its global health efforts under the AFGHS, including which MOU countries will be the focus of this work, which global health areas have been selected for cross-cutting support, and what objectives and activities might be supported with more focused, additional support within and beyond MOU countries. Still, the APS process remains underway, and additional addenda are expected as part of the last funding round. At this time, no awards have been publicly announced, and it is not known what will actually be funded. How this APS mechanism and specific awards ultimately operate to support or supplement the MOUs and other aspects of the AFGHS will be important to monitor going forward.
 Introduction
 Starting early on during his second administration, President Trump made a number of sweeping changes to U.S. foreign aid , which reverberated across U.S. and broader global health efforts. These included the reduction in the number of supported projects and organizations, dissolution of the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID), and the shifting of responsibility for remaining efforts to the State Department. In September 2025, following months of uncertainty, the State Department launched the America First Global Health Strategy (AFGHS), outlining a fundamental shift in how the U.S. is planning to carry out its global health work. This new approach is anchored to bilateral agreements negotiated directly with countries receiving U.S. global health assistance. To date, 36 such agreements, through Memoranda of Understanding (MOUs) totaling $26.7 billion, have been signed (although limited information is available on their status), with their implementation plans to come. These bilateral agreements each identify and prioritize global health needs to be financed jointly by the U.S. and partner country, with the U.S. committing $15.9 billion and partner countries committing to co-invest $10.3 billion so far. 1 The State Department has indicated that a main mechanism for implementing the MOUs will be through government-to-government (G2G) funding agreements, although these are still nascent and expected to take some time to develop. As such, the Department has also released – through an “Annual Program Statement” (APS), an open-ended competitive funding mechanism – a supplemental framework to support MOU implementation called the “ Advancing Global Health APS ” (AGH/APS) to solicit applications in support of AFGHS goals.
 Announced in March 2026, the State Department anticipates using the AGH/APS to provide up to $4.5 billion (subject to the availability of funds) over four funding windows from March 2026 through February 2027, with awards ranging from $500,000 to $250 million over 5 years. Some of the funding will be part of a country’s overall MOU funding envelope, while other funding may sit outside this envelope. Eligible applicants are U.S. and foreign private for-profit enterprises; U.S. and foreign public and private institutions of higher education; U.S and foreign organizations, including faith-based organizations; Public International Organizations (PIOs); and governmental institutions.
 To shed greater light on U.S. global health efforts under the AFGHS, this policy brief provides an analysis of the AGH/APS award opportunities (“addenda”) announced to date by looking at how funding may be directed across countries and selected areas of global health programming, painting a fuller picture of how continued U.S. global health investment may look in a post-USAID foreign aid landscape.
 Analysis
 As of November 2026, 12 addenda with up to 122 possible awards have been announced across three funding rounds, totaling up to $1.43 billion (see Box 1 ). This funding represents almost a third (32%) of the anticipated funding of $4.5 billion. Addenda include both country- and area-specific solicitations.

 Of the 12 addenda (see Figure 1 and Tables 1-2 ):
 seven identify specific countries for potential funding – Cameroon, Cote d’Ivoire, Malawi, Mozambique, Nigeria, the Philippines, and Uganda (all seven countries have signed MOUs with the U.S. 4 over the past year). Slightly more than half (54%, up to 66 awards) of potential awards and about half (51%, up to $730 million) of total announced funding are for country-specific addenda, which will be supported by funding that falls under the announced MOU funding envelopes. The largest number of potential awards are for Nigeria (up to 20), followed by Mozambique and Uganda (up to 15 each). The largest amounts of potential funding are for the Philippines and Nigeria (up to $200 million each), followed by Mozambique (up to $180 million). Across the seven countries, $7.3 billion in U.S. government funding is expected to be provided under their bilateral U.S. global health MOUs ; as such, the funding in the addenda could represent a potential 10% (up to $730 million) of this MOU funding.
 five identify specific areas for potential funding – child development, care, and protection; neglected tropical diseases, or NTDs; nutrition; rapid outbreak response; and population-based surveys and surveillance. Slightly less than half (46%, up to 56 awards) of potential awards and about half of funding (49%, up to $700 million) are for area-specific addenda, which are expected to be supported by funding that is outside of the MOUs. The largest number of potential awards are for NTDs (up to 25), followed by nutrition (12) and rapid outbreak response (10). The largest amounts of potential funding are for rapid outbreak response (up to $290 million), followed by NTDs (up to $162 million) and nutrition (up to $115 million).

 These addenda specify a range of objectives and activities, target populations, and, in some cases, particular geographic areas and countries. See Tables 1-2 and Appendix .
 Across the seven country-specific addenda (see Table 1 and Appendix Table 1 ):
 Objectives are varied and range from enhancing the delivery of health services across disease programs and improving country supply chain systems; to building government capacity to manage and sustain health programs and functions including financing, surveillance, and data systems. Specifically:
 Cameroon – using a One Health approach, aims to strengthen integrated public health systems in order to ensure global health security and strengthen outbreak and other emergency preparedness and response systems.
 Cote d’Ivoire – aims to strengthen disease surveillance, detection, and response to prevent cross-border spread; enhance integrated health service delivery across disease programs in order to improve efficiency; provide integrated technical support to strengthen management capacity across levels of health governance to support localized, community-centered health delivery; and sustain integrated service delivery in faith- and community-based facilities.
 Malawi – aims to provide strategic assistance to strengthen management capacity across several levels of health governance to standardize and support integrated service delivery platforms and transition responsibilities to the government; strengthen the government’s integrated health commodity supply chain system to ensure sustained commodity availability across all public health programs; and strengthen data systems integration and interoperability for data-driven decision making and sustained government-led digital health coordination and oversight.
 Mozambique – aims to strengthen integrated service delivery and support transition of functions to the government; enhance global health security through integrated disease surveillance and outbreak response; strengthen and scale interoperable digital health systems, and operationalize data-driven decision-making; and strengthen integrated supply chain systems, health systems, and institutional capacity for sustainable service delivery, including integrated health delivery in the Gorongosa district.
 Nigeria – aims to enhance faith- and community-based health service delivery; expand health insurance access for women, children, and their families; enhance global health security through disease surveillance and outbreak response; strengthen digital health systems, supply chains, laboratory networks, and health infrastructure; and improve health workforce financing.
 The Philippines –aims to strengthen disease surveillance and outbreak response to prevent cross-border spread; integrate health service delivery across disease programs to improve efficiency; strengthen domestic capacity to fund and manage health systems; and establish performance accountability mechanisms to monitor service delivery, epidemiology, supply chain, and domestic resource mobilization.
 Uganda –aims to support sustainable faith- and community-based health systems through establishing and scaling health financing mechanisms, sustaining integrated service delivery, building organization and network capacity; and to support enabling systems for accountable, government-led programming through strengthening and scaling interoperable, fit-for-purpose digital health systems, expanding sustainable power solutions for health facilities, institutionalizing supply chain improvements, conducting district-level risk assessments and independent verification for performance-based financing, and providing indoor residual spraying (IR) quality assurance.
 Activities in support of these objectives include, for example, strengthening disease surveillance, laboratory capacity, supply chain systems, and integrated health service delivery; scaling digital health systems to improve data use and sharing; training and support for health workforce management, planning, and retention; increasing quality assurance; supporting community platforms; improving infrastructure; and enhancing sustainable financing and accountability mechanisms.
 Some addenda mention key, focus, and vulnerable populations to include or target, such as vulnerable populations (including underserved communities, rural populations, women and children, and people living with HIV, tuberculosis, and malaria) in Mozambique and Nigeria; and high-risk populations (including “underserved, fragile and high-risk areas” and “populations with the greatest disease burden”) in the Philippines.
 While most country addenda mention working with faith-based organizations, three addenda – Cote d’Ivoire, Nigeria, and Uganda – specifically emphasize strengthening partnerships with faith-based organizations and cite them directly in their objectives.
 Across the five area-specific addenda (see Table 2 and Appendix Table 2 ):
 Objectives range from scaling and implementing programs addressing nutrition and child development to supporting high-impact NTD interventions, and from expanding routine and programmatic surveillance systems to building stronger outbreak detection and response capacity. Specifically:
 Child Development, Care, and Protection –aims to strengthen child protection systems; implement comprehensive programs to prevent malnutrition and poor development during the critical 1000 days (conception to age two), including interventions fostering secure, stimulating parent-child relationships; and prevent child-family separation and reduce reliance on residential care.
 NTDs –aims to accelerate the elimination of priority NTDs through integrated, high-impact interventions.
 Nutrition –aims to deliver integrated, high-impact, scalable, and sustainable nutrition services through existing health and community platforms (e.g., maternal and child health, HIV, tuberculosis or TB, malaria, immunization, and community health platforms).
 Population-Based Surveys and Surveillance –aims to advance innovative population-based survey methodologies and build strengthened routine and programmatic surveillance systems.
 Rapid Outbreak Response –aims to enhance rapid activation and surge response; improve early detection, containment, and mitigation; strengthen coordinated and operationally effective response; and build capacities that reinforce the system and support transition.
 Activities in support of these objectives include strengthening the systems and workforce that protect vulnerable children through improved laws, policies, and services; providing intensive support to the most vulnerable children and their families, alongside broader comprehensive efforts to focus on the first 1,000 days of children’s lives; delivering high-impact nutrition interventions, such as maternal nutrition and prenatal micronutrient supplementation; supporting the elimination of NTDs through strengthened laboratories, surveillance, and diagnostics; modernizing population health data systems; and strengthening global health security through improved infection prevention and control, immunization for outbreak response, point-of-entry screening, and risk communication.
 As with the country addenda, some include specific mention of key, focus, and vulnerable populations to include or target, such as children (including children under 2 and “children vulnerable to violence, exploitation, abuse, and neglect”) under the Child Development addendum; and high- and at-risk populations as a group for which it is important to ensure data is captured under surveillance projects, under the Population-Based Surveys and Surveillance addendum. 
 Two addenda identify specific geographic areas and countries for support (the remaining three are not specific):
 The NTDs addendum identifies 10 countries in the Western Hemisphere, 18 countries in Africa, and four countries in Asia and the Pacific; of these 32 countries, 11 have not signed MOUs, though some may do so at a future time; 5 and
 The nutrition addendum identifies 11 countries in Africa and 1 country in the Western Hemisphere; of these 12 countries, 2 have not signed MOUs. 6 
 These findings provide insight into how the U.S. intends to further operationalize its global health efforts under the AFGHS, including which MOU countries will be the focus of this work, which global health areas have been selected for cross-cutting support, and what objectives and activities might be supported with more focused, additional support within and beyond MOU countries. Still, the APS process remains underway, and additional addenda are expected as part of the last funding round. At this time, no awards have been publicly announced, 7 and it is not known what will actually be funded. How this APS mechanism and specific awards ultimately operate to support or supplement the MOUs and other aspects of the AFGHS will be important to monitor going forward.
